parts.note: a duke is addressed as 'Your Grace', and the leaves of a certain soft red fruit decorate a ducal coronet

explanation.surface: A pious phrase about the spiritual harvest of divine favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grace' reads as divine favour, but it is the style of a duke, whose coronet carries this fruit's leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: The ducal coronet is ornamented with leaves of this red summer berry, so it is the fruit belonging to a Grace.

parts.note: the wolf in the proverb goes about in the clothing of a meek farm animal

explanation.surface: A guileless person unwittingly supplies a costume to a wolf.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverbial wolf in sheep's clothing borrows its disguise from this harmless animal; 'lupine' means wolfish.
explanation.definitionFit: The meek woolly flock animal is a byword for innocence, and its fleece clothes the wolf in the proverb.

parts.note: read as two words it is a measure limiting beer, which the Chancellor's Budget did not ask for

explanation.surface: A complaint that the Chancellor's Budget lacks any sense.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as RATION ALE, a restriction on beer that the Budget did not call for; read whole, the word means reasoning, matching 'Logic'.
explanation.definitionFit: The underlying reasoning or justification for something is its logic.

parts.note: a fog signal gives a bang, called a report, and a forecast of fog is a kind of meteorological bulletin

explanation.walkthrough: A detonator used as a railway fog signal makes a report (a bang); the plural of that word also means bulletins on the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Forecasts announcing fog are bulletins about the atmosphere, and a report is also the bang of a fog signal.

clue.text: The proper ties, in a word, of which matrimony is one

definitions.text: The proper ties, in a word
definitions.meaning: 'proper ties' run together into one word gives properties, landed holdings
the marriage service speaks of the holy state of matrimony

explanation.surface: Musings on the correct bonds, of which marriage is one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a word' joins 'proper ties' into PROPERTIES, landed holdings; the Prayer Book calls marriage 'the holy estate of matrimony'.
explanation.definitionFit: Landed properties are large holdings of land, and the Prayer Book calls marriage a holy condition of life.

clue.text: She's responsible for an old fiddle with an accountant

parts.note: the rebec was a medieval bowed stringed instrument
CA stands for chartered accountant

explanation.surface: A woman is to blame for a fraud committed together with a bookkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fiddle' suggests a swindle, but it is the violin's ancestor, the rebec. 'She' is a girl's name; 'responsible for' links it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's name stands for any 'she', here a Biblical and literary heroine's name.

clue.text: One false step and the excursionist' has had it !

definitions.meaning: a stumble or slip of the foot
someone on an excursion has been on a short journey or outing

explanation.surface: A warning that one stumble will finish off the day-tripper.
explanation.definitionFit: A stumble is a slip of the foot, and an outing or jaunt is what any excursionist takes.

clue.text: What riders did on the roundabout was spectacular

parts.note: riders rode their horses
a roundabout is a ring, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Horsemen's antics on the fairground merry-go-round were impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roundabout' suggests a fairground ride, but it is just a circle, O. 'spectacular' is a noun, a show, as in a TV spectacular.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy show of riding and roping is a public spectacle, so a spectacular in the noun sense.

clue.text: Dickens's committee lady has the girl paged

indicators.note: the lady has, that is is made of, the letters of girl paged once they are reorganised

explanation.surface: A Dickensian committee woman has a girl summoned over the loudspeaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' asks for GIRL PAGED rearranged. Mrs Pardiggle is the bossy charity visitor in Dickens's Bleak House.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Pardiggle in Bleak House is a busy charitable committee woman forever doing good works.

parts.note: a hopeless pursuit, described as a bird-hunter's chase after an untamed bird

explanation.walkthrough: Fowlers are bird-catchers; the idiom for a pointless pursuit is literally a chase after a wild bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a hopeless, pointless pursuit pictures hunters chasing a wild bird.

definitions.meaning: a concentrated essence, as of a plant or meat
a quoted section taken from a book

explanation.surface: An instruction to focus your attention on the reading set.
explanation.definitionFit: An essence drawn out of something is a concentrate, and a selection quoted from a text is likewise one.

parts.note: Ibsen's play The Master ___ names the trade of its hero Solness

explanation.walkthrough: Ibsen's play is The Master Builder; the clue's 'master' points to the word that follows it in the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Halvard Solness, the title figure of Ibsen's play, is a master of the construction trade.

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Hamlet's cry on hearing from the Ghost that Claudius murdered his father

explanation.surface: Hamlet exclaims on learning that his uncle is the murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet, Act 1 scene 5: his soul had foreseen the truth about his uncle before the Ghost told it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet means his soul had foretold the truth, so the missing adjective means foreseeing or predictive.

clue.text: I'd get hot in this scanty garment !

indicators.note: the words I'd and hot get shaken up, 'get' signalling that they are turned into something new

parts.note: taken as its letters, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone remarks they would overheat wearing such skimpy clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get' rearranges ID and HOT into the Indian loincloth.
explanation.definitionFit: This Hindu loincloth, wrapped round the waist and legs, is a scanty piece of clothing.

clue.text: Robin whose absence was lamented tunefully

definitions.text: Robin whose absence was lamented tunefully

parts.words: Robin whose absence was lamented tunefully
parts.note: Robin is a man's name here, not a bird: the old song asks what's this dull town to me with Robin not here

explanation.surface: A songbird is missed and mourned in music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Robin' looks like the bird; it is the man of the Irish song 'Robin ___', which laments his absence.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad 'Robin Adair' mourns the absent man of its title.

parts.note: one word that is both an adjective for theoretical and a noun for summaries of papers

explanation.walkthrough: The word means theoretical as an adjective and, as a plural noun, summaries of papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Short summaries of papers bear this name, and as an adjective the word means theoretical rather than concrete.

parts.note: zest is a flavouring from citrus peel, so adding zest is a kind of flavouring work

explanation.walkthrough: 'zestful' suggests energetic enthusiasm; it means adding zest, the flavouring.
explanation.definitionFit: Flavouring food with salt, spice or zest is the act of making it tasty.

parts.note: a medieval pardoner sold remissions of sin, called by a word that also means lenient pampering

explanation.surface: A forgiving person's pleasant outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaucer's Pardoner sold indulgences; the adjective from that word also means lenient and pampering.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lenient and pampering is gratifying others' wishes, and indulgences were what a pardoner sold.

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go about, that is around, the word for nightfall
to break the word gates is to smash its letters and reassemble them

parts.note: even is a poetic word for evening

explanation.surface: Instructions to smash down some gates once darkness falls at this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' turns GATES into STAGE, which goes 'about' EVEN, giving ST-EVEN-AGE; 'here' is the definition, the place itself. STEVENAGE is a town in Hertfordshire, England, the first of the post-war New Towns.
explanation.definitionFit: A clue ending in 'here' defines a place name; this Hertfordshire new town is that place.

parts.note: Marcus Aurelius suggests a Roman woman's name formed from the Latin word for golden

explanation.surface: A precious partner chosen for a man called Marcus.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin aureus means golden; the Roman family name Aurelius, as in Marcus Aurelius, has a female form.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman female form of Aurelius, from the Latin for gold, would suit the wife of a Marcus Aurelius.

clue.text: Dice men can be a regular pest

indicators.note: the letters of dice men can be made into a different word when reordered

explanation.surface: Gamblers who throw dice can be a constant nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' rearranges DICE MEN. The answer, as a noun, is a disease always present in a region, a pest that is regular there.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease permanently present in a region is constantly there, a plague that never leaves.

clue.text: " The is wither'd from the lake " (Keats)

definitions.text: " The is wither'd from the lake " (Keats)

parts.words: " The is wither'd from the lake " (Keats)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Keats's La Belle Dame sans Merci, where a plant by the water has died back

explanation.surface: A line of Keats describing a bleak lakeside where plants have died.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats, La Belle Dame sans Merci: 'The sedge has wither'd from the lake, And no birds sing.' The blank is missing from the line as held.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a grassy waterside plant, the kind that grows on the margins of lakes.

clue.text: It's just right for the reader

definitions.text: It's just right for the reader

parts.words: It's just right for the reader
parts.note: the right-hand page of an open book, the one a reader faces on the right

explanation.surface: Something perfectly suited to a person who reads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just right' suggests 'ideal'; it means literally on the right, the right-hand page of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Printers call the right-hand page of an open book by this Latin term, the side facing the reader on the right.

parts.note: the word means men, and also the jaws or cheeks, so these fellows are literally of the cheek

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' suggests impudent, but the word for men also means the cheeks or jaws, as in Bath chaps.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal word for men or blokes also means the jaws or cheeks of an animal.

clue.text: Makes fun of Moli re's bluestockings?

definitions.meaning: Molière's comedy Les Précieuses ___ satirises pretentious literary ladies

explanation.surface: A remark about the French playwright mocking learned women.
explanation.walkthrough: Molière's play is Les Précieuses ridicules, whose précieuses are pretentious would-be intellectual women; the French adjective doubles as the English verb for mocking.
explanation.definitionFit: To mock is to deride, and the adjective in Molière's title describing his laughable affected ladies has the same spelling.

clue.text: " That was, to this, Hyperion to a" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: " That was, to this, Hyperion to a" (Hamlet)

parts.words: " That was, to this, Hyperion to a" (Hamlet)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Hamlet compares his godlike father to the goatish lecher Claudius

explanation.surface: Hamlet contrasts his dead father with his uncle.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet, Act 1 scene 2: 'So excellent a king, that was, to this, Hyperion to a satyr.' The blank is missing from the line as held.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a lustful half-goat woodland creature of Greek myth, set against the sun god Hyperion.

parts.note: personal property in law: a movable possession, as opposed to land

explanation.walkthrough: 'personal' suggests private feelings; in law personal property means movable goods.
explanation.definitionFit: In law a movable possession counts as personal property rather than real estate.

clue.text: Like the flower inspiring Wordsworth's deepest thoughts

definitions.text: Like the flower inspiring Wordsworth's deepest thoughts

parts.words: Like the flower inspiring Wordsworth's deepest thoughts
parts.note: the close of Wordsworth's Intimations Ode says the humblest bloom can give thoughts that lie too deep for tears

explanation.surface: A question about which bloom moved the poet Wordsworth most profoundly.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth, Intimations of Immortality: 'To me the meanest flower that blows can give Thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears.'
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth calls the flower the humblest or lowliest of all, the superlative of low and poor.

indicators.note: doubly says the word for therefore is written out two times

parts.note: so means therefore, as in 'so it follows'

explanation.surface: A remark that something is twice as middling, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doubly' repeats SO, the word for 'therefore'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something middling or only passable is called mediocre.

parts.note: the cathedral city of Trollope's novel ___ Towers and his Chronicles of Barsetshire

explanation.surface: A city famous for its tall buildings and recorded history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'towers' and 'chronicles' look like architecture and history; they are Trollope's titles Barchester Towers and the Chronicles of Barsetshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's imaginary cathedral city gives its name to Barchester Towers and is the centre of his Barsetshire novels.
